task.title: Evaluate orchestration libraries — confirm thin-core
acceptance_criteria: Each candidate skimmed for whether it offers anything the thin OTP core doesn't
A written build-vs-adopt decision with rationale
Any borrowed design ideas are recorded with their source
A determination on whether `claude_code` / `codex_sdk` are CLI wrappers or native reimplementations, with a uniform-Ports-vs-SDK recommendation
out_of_scope: Writing any adapter or orchestration code — this task is evaluation only
Adding any candidate library as a dependency
task.body: Skim the source and docs of the candidate Elixir orchestration libraries — `opal`, `gen_agent` + `gen_agent_ensemble`, `altar_ai`, `ex_mcp`. The harness core is deliberately thin — a Port per run, a `gen_statem` per run, a `DynamicSupervisor` for batches, all stock OTP — and harness no longer needs a normalized event model, so the expected outcome is build-thin-core rather than adopt. Confirm that, and record any design ideas worth borrowing. Also settle the per-agent SDK question: determine whether `claude_code` and `codex_sdk` are CLI wrappers around the headless binary or native reimplementations. If they are wrappers, harness gains nothing from them — its raw-passthrough design discards an SDK's normalized event model, and OTP Ports already spawn the binary with better termination signals — so every adapter uses uniform Ports; only a native reimplementation that removes the external-binary dependency would justify the dep. Record both decisions in a concept doc.
task.implemented: Evaluated opal, gen_agent, gen_agent_ensemble, altar_ai, ex_mcp + the claude_code/codex_sdk SDKs. Outcome: build thin core, adopt none, uniform Ports for all adapters. claude_code and codex_sdk confirmed CLI wrappers (not native reimpls). Decision + borrowed design ideas recorded in docs/orchestration-library-evaluation.md.

task.title: Define the AgentAdapter behaviour — invocation + capture
acceptance_criteria: An `AgentAdapter` behaviour with documented callbacks for invoke / capture / terminate
Raw agent output is passed through untouched — no per-agent event normalization
A capability declaration each adapter fills in
Nothing Claude-specific leaks into the contract
out_of_scope: Building any concrete adapter
Any normalized or typed event model — explicitly cut
task.body: Define the core contract every agent adapter implements — a `behaviour` that, given a task spec plus run options, builds the agent's headless command line, spawns it, detects termination, and hands back the raw captured output plus wall-clock duration. Deliberately no normalized event model: harness does not parse or remap each agent's JSON — the consumer is an AI that reads raw transcripts natively, and harness derives run success from its own verification stack, not the agent's self-reported result. The behaviour also declares per-adapter capabilities (session resume, permission modes, and so on). Contract only — no concrete adapter.
task.implemented: Defined the Harness.AgentAdapter behaviour: 4 callbacks (capabilities/0, build_command/1, classify_message/2, terminate/1) plus generic AgentAdapter.invoke/2 (Port spawn) and supports?/2. Structs: Invocation, Run, Capabilities. Raw passthrough, no event model; :error vs :terminated split for retry classification; session-token extraction and version/0 probe deferred. No concrete adapter. The use-macro from the plan was dropped — Doctor's 100% spec gate does not pair @spec to a defmacro; adapters declare @behaviour directly.

task.title: Build the Claude Code headless adapter
acceptance_criteria: A headless prompt run captures raw output and reports termination
Working directory and permission mode are wired
Session resume works across two runs
Termination is derived from process exit + timeout, not `$?`
An idle timeout kills a run that emits no output for a configurable window, separate from the total-run budget
task.body: Implement the first concrete adapter — driving Claude Code headlessly via `claude -p` over Ports. Capture the raw output stream and hand it back unparsed. Wire working directory, permission mode, and session resume/continue. Detect termination from the process/Port closing plus two timeout guards — a total-run budget, and an idle timeout that kills a run emitting no output for a configurable window — never from the exit code, which is known to be unreliable.
task.implemented: Built Harness.AgentAdapter.Claude (claude -p, stream-json, --permission-mode bypassPermissions, --continue resume), the generic Harness.AgentAdapter.Driver enforcing total + idle timeout guards, the Outcome result struct, and the shared OSProcess port-lifecycle helper. Resume resolves the behaviour's session-token deferral via --continue (no new callback). 100% test + doc coverage; integration test green against real claude.

task.title: Worktree-per-job lifecycle
acceptance_criteria: Each run gets its own isolated git worktree
Concurrent runs do not collide on the working tree
Worktrees are cleaned up on success and retained on failure (configurable)
A crashed run does not leak an orphan worktree
task.body: harness runs every job in an isolated git worktree so concurrent agent runs never collide and the verification stack has a clean checkout to grade. Implement worktree creation per run, dispatch of the agent into it, and a keep-or-tear-down decision on completion (retain on failure for inspection; configurable). This is the automation of the repo's existing worktree-per-branch convention.
task.implemented: Harness.Worktree (create/2, finish/3, remove/1, retained?/1, base_dir/1) for per-run isolated git worktrees + Harness.Worktree.Sweeper boot-time orphan reaper. Harness.Git subprocess wrapper. Configurable via :harness, :worktree app env + HARNESS_WORKTREE_ROOT. 48 tests, coverage 100/93.6/85.2%.

task.title: rmap task ingestion
acceptance_criteria: harness fetches a task — by id, or the next pending one — from the rmap roadmap
The task renders to an agent-ready prompt suitable for the adapter
Ingestion reads the rmap source — it does not duplicate the roadmap
task.body: Let harness pull a task straight from the rmap roadmap — read `roadmap/tasks.toml` / `roadmap/data.json` (or shell out to `rmap`) and render the task as a ready-to-run agent prompt. `rmap delegate <id> --to <agent>` already emits a paste-ready prompt; harness consumes that instead of a human copy-pasting it. This is the input half of the loop — the roadmap becomes the job queue.
task.implemented: Added Harness.Roadmap.ingest/2 + Harness.Roadmap.Item. Shells out to rmap (show/next/delegate) with explicit --tasks-path; fetches a task by id or next-pending and renders the rmap delegate prompt verbatim. Error taxonomy: invalid_agent/invalid_selector/rmap_not_found/no_pending_task/task_not_found/roadmap_not_found/rmap_failed/rmap_bad_output. Covered by a unit suite with fixture roadmaps under test/fixtures/.

task.title: Verification runner — run the target project's check stack
acceptance_criteria: A configurable list of check commands runs against a given worktree
An Elixir preset is provided as the default check set
Each check's pass/fail and output are captured into a structured verdict
Any red check makes the overall verdict red
out_of_scope: Feeding failures back to the agent — that is the autonomous repair loop task
task.body: After an agent finishes, harness runs the target project's own check stack against its worktree and produces a structured pass/fail — this is what makes "did the job succeed?" objective and agent-agnostic, instead of trusting the agent's self-report. The check set is a configurable list of commands; ship an Elixir preset (`mix test.json`, `mix dialyzer.json`, doctor, sobelow, credo). Aggregate each check's result into one verdict the run lifecycle can gate on.
task.implemented: Harness.Verification grades a worktree by running a configurable check stack and aggregating per-check Results into a Verdict (any red => red). Ships elixir_preset/0: mix test.json, dialyzer.json, credo --strict, doctor, sobelow --exit. Each check is spawned over an OTP port bounded by an absolute per-check deadline (default 600_000 ms) so a hung check — idle or still streaming output — is killed rather than wedging the run; System.cmd was rejected as uninterruptible and subprocess-orphaning. Each Result carries a kind (:exited | :timed_out | :not_launched) so a consumer can distinguish a retryable timeout from a genuine red check. Check/Result/Verdict structs + config under :harness, :verification. 19 tests, 94% coverage.

task.title: Supervised run lifecycle process
acceptance_criteria: One job = one supervised `gen_statem` with observable state
It drives worktree → adapter → verification and settles on a verdict
A crashing run is isolated from siblings
Per-run timeout and external cancellation both work
task.body: Implement the supervised process that owns one job end to end — model it as a `gen_statem` moving through `dispatched → running → verifying → {done | failed}`. It creates the worktree, spawns the adapter, waits for termination, runs the verification stack, and settles on a verdict. Crash isolation (a failed run never touches siblings), a per-run timeout, and external cancellation. The run state must be observable. Completing this task is the single-agent core loop working end to end for one task; the contract-proof bundle (conformance suite + Codex adapter) then proves the adapter contract holds on a second agent.
task.implemented: Harness.Run :gen_statem owns one job end to end (dispatched → running → verifying → done/failed): carves the isolated worktree, dispatches the agent via AgentAdapter.Driver, runs the verification stack, settles a verdict. Harness.Run.Supervisor (one_for_one DynamicSupervisor, :temporary children) gives crash isolation between concurrent runs; a Registry maps run-id → pid; a Task.Supervisor parents every per-step async task so a crashing step is an event, not a crash. cancel/1 and a per-run lifetime-budget timeout both abort cleanly and SIGKILL the agent; status/1 exposes live state. AgentAdapter.Driver gained an :on_spawn hook so the lifecycle process can capture the run handle for cancellation. Verification is the sole grader — a timed-out agent is still verified. 23 new tests; suite green; dialyzer/credo/doctor clean.

task.title: Batch orchestrator with concurrency cap
acceptance_criteria: A batch of N tasks runs under a concurrency cap of M
Partial failure is tolerated — the batch completes and reports per-task status
Per-task verdicts are collected into one batch result
task.body: Implement the batch layer — fan a set of tasks out across run-lifecycle processes under a `DynamicSupervisor`, with a configurable concurrency cap, and collect the per-task verdicts. Tolerate partial failure: one failed or red run must not abort the batch; the batch result reports every task's outcome. A batch is typically an rmap bundle or an `rmap next-bundle` result.
task.implemented: Harness.Batch.run/4 + Harness.Batch.Result — fans tasks out across supervised Harness.Run children under a concurrency cap, tolerates partial failure (red/crashed run never aborts the batch), collects one Run.Result per task in input order. Delivered via parallel multi-agent dogfood, driven by Codex; commit on harness/run-1779373868703-29f9a9b0.

task.title: Retry policy with failure classification
acceptance_criteria: Failures are classified as transient, quota-exhausted, or terminal
Transient failures retry with capped exponential backoff
Quota exhaustion stops retrying that agent at once — no backoff loop against a multi-hour wall
Terminal failures are not retried
The policy is configurable per batch or per run
task.body: Add a per-run retry policy that first classifies the failure. Transient failures (a process crash, a flaky check) retry with capped exponential backoff. Quota exhaustion — a subscription agent hitting its cap — is NOT retryable on a useful timescale (the reset window is hours); it must stop retrying that agent immediately, marked for fail-over rather than backoff. Genuine terminal task failures are never retried. Make the policy injectable per batch or per run.
task.implemented: Harness.Run.RetryPolicy + Harness.Run.FailureClass — classifies a failed run transient/quota_exhausted/terminal; transient retries with capped exponential backoff, quota stops at once for fail-over, terminal never retried; policy injectable per run/batch via :harness, :retry_policy. Delivered via parallel multi-agent dogfood, driven by Cursor; commit on harness/run-1779373868714-f42cdd07.

task.title: Autonomous repair loop
acceptance_criteria: A red verdict triggers a repair attempt — failures fed back via session resume
The loop stops on green or at the attempt cap
A quota or terminal failure ends the loop instead of burning attempts
The number of repair attempts is configurable
task.body: Close the verify loop. When verification comes back red, feed the failing checks' output back to the same agent via session resume and re-run, up to a configurable attempt cap. The objective check stack is the grader, so an agent iterating against it is not self-grading. Stop on green, on the attempt cap, or on a non-repairable failure class (e.g. quota exhaustion — hand to fail-over instead).
task.implemented: Harness.Run repair loop + Harness.Run.RepairPrompt — a red verdict resumes the same agent with the failing checks fed back, re-commits and re-grades up to :max_repair_attempts (default 2); stops on green, the cap, or a non-repairable failure. Delivered via parallel multi-agent dogfood, driven by Claude; commit on harness/run-1779373868724-a4ceeede.

task.title: Reusable adapter conformance test suite

The Claude adapter passes the full suite
Invocation, capture, termination, timeout, and adapter-level cancellation (`terminate` kills an in-flight run) are all covered
task.body: Build a reusable test module every `AgentAdapter` implementation must pass — exercising invocation, raw-output capture, termination detection, timeout, and adapter-level cancellation (the behaviour's `terminate` callback killing an in-flight run and releasing its Port/process). This is adapter-scope only: external cancellation *orchestration* — a caller telling the running system to cancel a job — is the supervised lifecycle's concern (Task 8) and is out of scope here. Run the Claude adapter against the suite. This suite is the gate Codex and every later adapter (Cursor, Grok, ACP) are held to: a leak gets fixed in the behaviour, not patched around in the adapter.

Contract checks are agent-free (synthesized port messages + /bin/sleep stand-in); one :integration test drives the real agent through Driver.run/3. Run against the Claude adapter (ClaudeConformanceTest) and Harness.FakeAdapter (FakeAdapterConformanceTest, proving reusability). task.title: Capability + availability registry with quota fail-over
acceptance_criteria: Each adapter declares its capabilities
A run requesting an unsupported capability is rejected up front, not mid-run
A quota-exhausted agent is marked unavailable and the job fails over to a capable agent with headroom
Fail-over routing is observable
task.body: Add a registry the orchestrator queries before dispatch. Each adapter declares its capabilities (session resume, permission granularity, MCP/tool config, and so on) so a run requesting an unsupported capability is rejected up front with a clear error. The registry also tracks availability — when an agent hits its subscription quota, the orchestrator routes the job to another agent with headroom instead of failing it. This is the concrete payoff of running multiple adapters.
task.implemented: Harness.AgentRegistry — declarative per-adapter capability listing + availability state. Harness.Batch and Harness.Run.Supervisor gain a capability check before dispatch: a run requesting an unsupported capability is rejected up front, never mid-run. A quota-exhausted agent is marked unavailable and the batch routes its task to another capable adapter with headroom; fail-over routing is observable via Batch.Result events. Delivered by Codex in the Round-2 dogfood batch (run-1779511173217-4909d4fd); repair loop fired once (credo 120-char line-length) before 5/5 verification green. Shipped in 9b686a9.

task.title: Inject a harness-owned rule set into agent invocations
acceptance_criteria: The harness holds one canonical rule set; no rule content is hand-maintained per repo or per agent

Each adapter injects the rule set through its best available channel — a dedicated system-prompt flag where the CLI offers one (Claude's --append-system-prompt-file), else prompt-prepend or a generated ephemeral rule file in the worktree
The injected set is a curated, filterable subset — verification gates are excluded, since the verification runner enforces them
Two different agents dispatched by harness receive the same canonical rules without a hand-maintained rule file per repo
out_of_scope: Verification-gate enforcement — coverage, dialyzer, and credo thresholds are the verification runner's job (Task 7), checked not injected
Editing or deleting the user's own ~/.claude/includes/ files — what the harness injects is a harness-side decision, independent of the user's personal Claude Code config

Hand-maintained, committed per-repo rule files (a CLAUDE.md / AGENTS.md / Cursor rules file checked into every target repo) — that maintenance burden is what this task replaces; a harness-generated ephemeral rule file, rendered from the canonical source into a throwaway worktree and never committed, is in scope as a delivery channel for CLIs with no system-prompt flag (Codex, Cursor)
task.body:
The harness owns one canonical set of working rules — the methodology and behavioral guidance currently scattered across a project's CLAUDE.md and its includes (minimalism, no-evasion, the pushback mandate, code-style KPIs, the implementer/reviewer handoff, niche tool references). Instead of every target repo carrying and hand-syncing a CLAUDE.md plus an AGENTS.md plus a Cursor rules file, the harness injects its rule set directly into each agent's headless invocation at dispatch time.

Injection is a per-adapter `build_command/1` concern: use the agent's dedicated system-prompt channel where it has one (Claude Code's `--append-system-prompt-file`), and where it does not, either prepend the rules to the task prompt or render them into a harness-generated ephemeral rule file in the throwaway worktree (Codex and Cursor read a native rule file; Grok has neither, so prompt-prepend). Every delivery is rendered from the one canonical source — what this task rules out is a hand-maintained rule file committed to each target repo, not a generated ephemeral one. The verified per-agent CLI surface is recorded in `docs/agent-cli-reference.md`.

The injected set is a curated, filterable subset, not a token dump: it carries methodology plus the harness's own operational instructions to a dispatched agent (you are being driven by harness; the verification stack is the grader; stage, don't self-grade). It deliberately excludes the verification gates — coverage thresholds, dialyzer-zero, credo-strict — because those are enforced by the verification runner (Task 7), not prose the agent is trusted to honor. A target repo's own CLAUDE.md still auto-loads for Claude; harness injection adds its operational layer and gives the other three agents the same rules without a hand-maintained per-agent file.
task.implemented: Added Harness.AgentRules (canonical rule set rendered from priv/agent_rules/canonical.md, curated-subset filtering — verification gates excluded since the verification runner enforces them) and Harness.AgentAdapter.RulesInjection (per-adapter injection helper). Every adapter build_command/1 wires the rule set through its best channel: Claude --append-system-prompt-file; Codex and Cursor render an ephemeral rule file into the worktree; Grok and Antigravity prompt-prepend. Delivered by Cursor in the Round-2 dogfood batch (run-1779511173207-ec889d74); repair loop fired once (sobelow directory-traversal findings) before 5/5 verification green. Shipped in 826aaff.

task.title: Give Port-spawned agents an immediate-EOF stdin
acceptance_criteria: A Port-spawned agent does not stall waiting on stdin
The prompt and argv are passed without shell-quoting hazards
The executable-not-found error path stays clear
task.body:
Headless agent CLIs spawned over an OTP port inherit an open-but-empty stdin pipe. An agent that peeks stdin to support `cat file | agent -p` then stalls waiting for input that never comes: the Claude Code adapter's integration test shows `claude` printing `no stdin data received in 3s, proceeding without it` and eating a flat 3s per run. Other agents (Cursor, Codex, Grok) likely behave the same.

Give every Port-spawned agent process a stdin that is immediately at EOF, so it proceeds without the stall. The clean, shell-quoting-safe approach is the `sh -c '...' "$@"` argv trick — spawn `/bin/sh` with script `exec <agent> "$@" </dev/null` and pass the real agent argv as positional parameters, so no prompt escaping is needed. Decide whether this belongs in the generic `Harness.AgentAdapter.invoke/2` spawn or per-adapter `build_command/1`; if it moves into the generic spawn, preserve the clean `{:error, {:executable_not_found, _}}` signal that the current direct `System.find_executable/1` provides.
task.implemented: Spawn every agent through /bin/sh with an exec wrapper redirecting stdin from /dev/null, so a Port-spawned headless CLI gets an immediate EOF instead of stalling and exiting doing nothing. Fix lives in the generic AgentAdapter Port spawn (not per-adapter); exec keeps the port os_pid the agent itself so terminate/1 still reaches it; executable+argv ride as sh positional parameters so the prompt needs no shell quoting; System.find_executable/1 still gates the executable-not-found path. FakeAdapter gained stdin_eof and echo-text fixtures; new agent_adapter tests cover stdin-EOF and argv-verbatim. Surfaced by the first dogfood run, which exited :no_changes. Suite green (126 incl. integration); dialyzer/credo/doctor/sobelow clean.

task.title: Commit the agent's work to the run branch before worktree teardown
acceptance_criteria: A :committing state runs between running and verifying; the agent's diff is committed to the harness/<id> branch
On a green run the worktree is torn down but the branch commit survives and carries the agent's files
An agent that produced no diff settles :failed with reason :no_changes (verification skipped)
A commit failure settles :failed with reason {:commit_failed, _}
Full suite green incl. new run/worktree tests; dialyzer/credo/doctor clean
task.body:
The dogfood path destroys the deliverable. A run carves a worktree + harness/<id> branch (Harness.Worktree.create), dispatches an agent that edits files in the worktree, runs verification against the working tree, and on a green verdict calls Worktree.finish(:success) -> git worktree remove --force -- which wipes the agent's uncommitted edits. Nothing in Harness.Run or the driver ever commits, so the harness/<id> branch stays at base ref with zero commits. Harness.Worktree's moduledoc claims the verified commits on the branch are the run's deliverable, but no commit is ever made. Existing run tests never caught this: FakeAdapter's :echo/:sleep commands write no files.

Fix: add a :committing lifecycle state to Harness.Run between running and verifying. When the agent terminates, commit the worktree's full diff to the harness/<id> branch via a new Harness.Worktree.commit/2, then verification grades the committed tree. Commit before verify, always. An agent that produced no diff settles :failed with reason :no_changes (verification skipped). This blocks all dogfooding and is the hand-built bootstrap that lets Task 12 onward be dispatched through harness itself. Discovered during Task 8 follow-up.
task.implemented: Added a :committing lifecycle state to Harness.Run between running and verifying, plus Harness.Worktree.commit/2. When the agent terminates, harness stages and commits the worktree's diff to the harness/<id> branch (explicit harness committer identity, set via git -c so it never fails on missing config) before verification grades it. An agent that produced no diff settles :failed/:no_changes (verification skipped); a commit error settles :failed/{:commit_failed, _}. The branch commit now survives finish/3 teardown — the deliverable is no longer destroyed. New reasons :no_changes and {:commit_failed,_} on Run.Result; :committing added to Run/Status state types. FakeAdapter gained :write/:write_then_hang/:break_git fixtures; new run + worktree tests cover commit, no-changes, commit-failure, and work-survives-teardown. Suite green (124 tests), dialyzer/credo/doctor clean.

task.title: Caller-controlled agent environment in the AgentAdapter contract
acceptance_criteria: A caller can add environment variables for a dispatched agent via `Invocation`, without mutating the orchestrator BEAM's own environment
A caller can remove an inherited environment variable for a dispatched agent — the dogfood `System.delete_env("ANTHROPIC_API_KEY")` workaround becomes unnecessary
The adapter conformance suite verifies both env injection and env scrubbing, and every adapter passes it
out_of_scope: Quota/billing detection or fail-over routing — marking a quota-exhausted agent unavailable is Task 16
Secret management or credential vaulting — harness passes through whatever env the caller specifies; it does not store credentials
task.body:
Harness Port-spawns every headless agent inheriting the orchestrator BEAM's environment wholesale — `Harness.AgentAdapter.spawn_run/5` opens the port layering only the adapter's `build_command/1` env additions on top, and `Harness.AgentAdapter.Invocation` carries no environment field at all. The operator has no lever to shape what a dispatched agent sees: they cannot add a per-run variable, and they cannot scrub an inherited one — e.g. remove an inherited `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` so `claude` falls back to its subscription OAuth credentials instead of a (possibly unfunded) API key. That exact gap forced the dogfood driver to call `System.delete_env/1` on the whole BEAM as a workaround.

Give the caller a first-class mechanism, carried on `Invocation`, to both set and unset environment variables for the spawned agent — threaded through every adapter's `build_command/1` and the port spawn (note `port_env/1` currently cannot express a removal: `{key, false}` would crash `String.to_charlist/1`). Cover it in the adapter conformance suite so every adapter honors it identically.
task.implemented: Added a caller-controlled env field to Harness.AgentAdapter.Invocation (map of name => string to set, name => false to scrub an inherited var). Threaded through every adapter's build_command/1 and into the port spawn via port_env/1 ({key, false} -> Erlang Port :env removal, fixing the String.to_charlist crash flagged in the task body). Plumbed as the :env opt on Harness.Run.Supervisor.start_run/4. Conformance suite gains a shared env injection+scrubbing test every adapter passes. Dogfood driver template updated to use env: %{ANTHROPIC_API_KEY => false} instead of System.delete_env. Delivered by Grok in the Round-1 dogfood batch — all 5 verification checks green.

task.title: Antigravity headless adapter
acceptance_criteria: Create Harness.AgentAdapter.Antigravity module implementing Harness.AgentAdapter behaviour
Implement capabilities/0 declaring support for :session_resume, :streaming_output, and :autonomous permission modes
Implement build_command/1 for Antigravity invocation, handling -p, --dangerously-skip-permissions, and --continue flags
Reject unsupported models with {:error, {:unsupported_model, model}}
Unit tests cover all capabilities, build_command/1 scenarios, and message classification
Integrate :antigravity into Harness.Roadmap and Harness.Roadmap.Item valid agents lists
task.body:
Support Antigravity CLI (`agy`) as a headless coding agent adapter in Harness.

The adapter will invoke the `agy` CLI using the `--print` (`-p`) flag for headless execution, `--dangerously-skip-permissions` for autonomous execution, and `--continue` (`-c`) for session resumption. The `agy` CLI does not support a custom model flag, so it will return `{:error, {:unsupported_model, model}}` if a model is specified.

The integration includes registering the `:antigravity` agent in `Harness.Roadmap` and `Harness.Roadmap.Item`, and verifying compliance via an adapter-specific unit test suite.
task.implemented: Created Harness.AgentAdapter.Antigravity module implementing the Harness.AgentAdapter behaviour, mapping autonomous permission mode to --dangerously-skip-permissions, supporting session resumption with --continue, and rejecting model overrides with {:error, {:unsupported_model, model}}. Integrated :antigravity into Harness.Roadmap and Harness.Roadmap.Item. Added unit tests and conformance tests under test/harness/agent_adapter/ verifying capabilities, build_command, and integration.

task.title: Hoist universal adapter callbacks into the AgentAdapter behaviour
acceptance_criteria: A new adapter implementing only build_command/1 + capabilities/0 compiles and passes the conformance suite
All existing adapters keep passing the conformance suite unchanged
Duplicated classify_message/2 and terminate/1 bodies are removed from the adapter modules
task.body: Building the Codex, Cursor, Grok and Antigravity adapters surfaced that classify_message/2, terminate/1, and the --model argv helper are byte-identical across every adapter (Claude, Codex, Cursor, Grok, Antigravity, FakeAdapter). Hoist them into the behaviour via `use Harness.AgentAdapter` + defoverridable, so a new adapter declares only what is genuinely agent-specific (build_command/1, capabilities/0). Not an abstraction leak — the contract held — but pure duplication every new adapter re-copies. Surfaced by the first parallel dogfood batch (Tasks 13-15).
task.implemented: Introduced `use Harness.AgentAdapter` + defoverridable defaults (top-level provider fns for classify/terminate + public model_args/1 helper). Switched all 6 adapters to `use` and removed duplicated bodies + unused aliases/helpers. Updated test MinimalAdapter + added coverage test. Full stack (295 tests 0 failures incl. all conformances, credo/dialyzer/doctor/sobelow clean) passes.

task.title: Wire the retry policy into the batch orchestrator
acceptance_criteria: A transient failure in a batch run is retried per the injected RetryPolicy before its result lands in the batch result
A quota-exhausted or terminal failure is not retried — it settles into the batch result immediately
The concurrency cap is respected while retries are in flight
The retry policy is injectable per batch and defaults from :harness, :retry_policy
out_of_scope: Quota fail-over to a different agent — that is the capability registry's job (Task 16)
The repair loop — Task 11's :verification_red feedback is distinct from transient-failure retry
task.body: Harness.Run.RetryPolicy (Task 10) ships as an injectable helper — RetryPolicy.run/2 wraps a `fn -> Result.t()` loop — but nothing calls it. Harness.Batch (Task 9) was built in the same parallel dogfood batch off the same HEAD, so it fans runs out but never applies the retry policy: a transient failure (a process crash, a flaky check) in a batch run is reported, not retried. Wire the retry policy into the batch orchestrator so each run's lifecycle is wrapped by RetryPolicy.run/2, with the policy injectable per batch via the :retry_policy opt already documented on Harness.Run.Supervisor.start_run/4. Transient failures retry with capped backoff; quota-exhausted and terminal failures are not retried — they settle into the batch result as-is. The concurrency cap must still hold while retries are in flight. Surfaced by the parallel multi-agent dogfood batch that delivered Tasks 9-11.
task.implemented: Rewrote Batch.fill_slots and follow-up dispatch hooks to delegate every Run start through RetryPolicy.run/2 — the orchestrator now consumes retry classifications natively, propagates max-attempts surrender as :failed, and exposes the wired-in policy via Batch.start_link opts. Added test coverage for the retry-then-succeed and retry-then-give-up paths, including transient (worktree) and quota classifications.

task.title: Force-settle the Run lifetime timeout when the agent handle never arrives
acceptance_criteria: A run whose `{:run_handle}` message never arrives still settles within `lifetime_timeout`
The settled `Result`/`Status` carries a failure reason identifying the never-spawned cause
An agent that spawned just before the lifetime timeout is still cleaned up (SIGKILL or handed to the sweeper)
A regression test drives the never-arrives path and asserts the run force-settles
out_of_scope: Changing the agent `total_timeout` / `idle_timeout` semantics
The repair-loop attempt cap
task.body:
`Harness.Run`'s last-resort lifetime budget (`lifetime_timeout`) currently only force-settles a run once the agent run handle has arrived. If the `{:run_handle}` message never arrives — a hung `build_command`/`invoke` before the agent spawns — the lifetime timeout defers instead of settling, so a wedged run can sit forever and the budget is not actually enforced.

Make the lifetime timeout the genuine last-resort guarantee: when it fires, the run settles (`:failed`, with a reason naming the never-spawned cause) regardless of whether a run handle exists yet. Decide and document the trade-off — force-settling may orphan a just-spawned agent to the `Worktree.Sweeper`, which is acceptable for a last-resort budget.

Surfaced by the post-merge audit of 53cc3ef — see `.audit/53cc3ef-supervised-run-lifecycle.md` finding 3 (a `discuss-design` divergence: Codex rated it pri 8, Claude assessed it latent for the shipped adapters).
task.implemented: lib/harness/run.ex lifetime-timeout handler force-settles the Run when the agent handle never arrives, covering the never-spawned race window; regression tests (run-1779588540043-7f1a6138)

task.title: Pin Worktree.commit/2 to the run's harness/<id> branch
acceptance_criteria: `commit/2` lands the commit on the run's `harness/<id>` branch even if the agent moved or detached HEAD, OR fails with a dedicated error rather than committing off-branch
The failure path returns a typed `Harness.Worktree` error and `Harness.Run` settles the run cleanly on it
A test simulates an agent moving HEAD and asserts the deliverable is not stranded
out_of_scope: Restricting which git operations the agent may run inside the worktree
task.body:
`Harness.Worktree.commit/2` captures the agent's work by committing whatever the worktree's HEAD currently points at. The whole deliverable model assumes the work lands on the run's `harness/<id>` branch — but an agent that runs `git switch` or detaches HEAD makes `commit/2` land the commit off-branch, and worktree teardown then loses the run's deliverable.

Make `commit/2` pin its commit to the worktree's own `harness/<id>` branch, or fail loudly if HEAD has moved. The audit noted three options — assert HEAD is on the expected branch and fail with a dedicated error, force-checkout the branch before committing, or commit against an explicit branch ref. Pick one and carry the ripple: a new `Harness.Worktree` error variant and the matching `committing`-state handling in `Harness.Run`.

Surfaced by the post-merge audit of f53b50c — see `.audit/f53b50c-commit-agent-delivery.md` (a `discuss-design` divergence; uncommon trigger but a real deliverable-loss gap).
task.implemented: lib/harness/worktree.ex Worktree.commit/2 now pins to the run's harness/<id> branch via explicit refspec; adds Worktree tests + run integration test (run-1779588540053-949e2796)

task.title: Resolve the rmap-delegate ingest gap for the Grok and Antigravity adapters
acceptance_criteria: A decision is recorded: extend `rmap delegate` to all adapters, or formalize the claude/codex/cursor-rendered-prompt contract for non-delegatable ones
If formalizing: `Harness.Roadmap`, the `@valid_agents` comment, and the agent-facing docs state the contract explicitly
If extending rmap: every harness adapter is a valid `ingest/2` agent, with a regression test per adapter
out_of_scope: Implementing new agent adapters
task.body:
`rmap delegate --to` accepts only `claude` / `codex` / `cursor`, and `Harness.Roadmap` deliberately shells out to `rmap delegate` to render task prompts — so `@valid_agents` on the ingest surface mirrors that set. harness now also ships Grok and Antigravity adapters, which have no ingest path: `ingest(agent: :grok)` / `ingest(agent: :antigravity)` are rejected by design, and those adapters run only with a claude/codex/cursor-rendered prompt dispatched directly via `Harness.Run.Supervisor.start_run/4`. This gap already produced one bug — the `:antigravity` value wrongly admitted to `@valid_agents`, fixed in the 25ed795 audit.

Resolve it deliberately: either extend rmap's `delegate --to` surface to cover every harness adapter, or formally accept that non-delegatable adapters run with a claude/codex/cursor-rendered prompt and document that contract clearly (in `Harness.Roadmap`, the `@valid_agents` rationale comment, and the dogfooding / agent-reference docs).

Surfaced by the post-merge audit of 25ed795 — see `.audit/25ed795-antigravity-headless-adapter.md`.
task.implemented: Formalized the non-delegatable-adapter contract: Grok/Antigravity run via a claude/codex/cursor-rendered prompt dispatched directly to their adapter module (not extending rmap — keeps the rmap Rust CLI decoupled). Documented in Harness.Roadmap moduledoc + @valid_agents comment, CLAUDE.md, docs/dogfooding-workflow.md, docs/agent-cli-reference.md. Delivered by Antigravity in the Round-1 dogfood batch; agy's worktree-isolation bug (Task 32) leaked the work into the main checkout — verified green by a separate evaluator pass (test 245 pass / credo 0 / doctor 100%).

task.title: Antigravity adapter does not isolate to its run worktree
acceptance_criteria: An Antigravity-driven harness run edits files only inside its run worktree; the main checkout stays clean
The Antigravity adapter moduledoc accurately describes how `agy` resolves its working directory
If `agy` cannot be headlessly constrained to one directory, that limitation is documented and Antigravity dispatch fails fast with a clear error instead of polluting the main checkout
A regression guard catches a future adapter that writes outside its run worktree
out_of_scope: Fixing the agy CLI upstream — harness works with the CLI as shipped
Grok / Claude / Codex / Cursor adapters — they isolate correctly
task.body:
During the Round-1 multi-agent dogfood batch (2026-05-22), Task 31 was driven by the Antigravity adapter. harness Port-spawned `agy` with the port `:cd` set to the run's isolated worktree, but `agy` edited files in the *main checkout* (`~/_DATA/code/harness/`) instead — the run settled `:no_changes` because the worktree had no diff, and the agent's actual work landed, ungraded, in the canonical checkout.

The Antigravity adapter moduledoc claims `agy` "inherits its working directory from the spawned process's cwd" — that is false. `agy --help` exposes no `--cwd` / `--workspace` / `--project` flag; the only directory control is `--add-dir` (repeatable, *additive* — it widens the workspace rather than replacing it). The Grok adapter also relies on Port cwd and isolated correctly in the same batch, so harness's worktree + `:cd` mechanism is sound — this is specific to `agy`'s workspace resolution (a configured/last-used workspace, or git-common-dir resolution following the worktree's `.git` file pointer back to the main checkout). Depends on Task 26 (the Antigravity adapter).

Investigate how `agy` actually resolves its working directory/workspace and make the Antigravity adapter guarantee the agent edits ONLY its run worktree. If `agy` cannot be headlessly constrained to a single directory, that is itself the finding — record it and gate Antigravity out of worktree-isolated dispatch with a clear up-front error, never silent main-checkout pollution. No dogfood run may write outside its worktree.

task.title: Same-task A/B agent-evaluation mode
acceptance_criteria: A caller dispatches one rmap task to N agents at once — each in its own isolated worktree — and gets back one result per agent
The comparison collects per-agent quality metrics (verdict, repair attempts, wall-clock, first-attempt failed-check count, agent diff size) side by side
The verification verdict stays a binary pass/fail — evaluation metrics are an additive layer, never folded into the verdict
Partial failure is tolerated — one agent's crashed or red run never aborts the comparison
out_of_scope: A weighted composite 'agent score' or leaderboard — surface the raw per-agent metrics; ranking stays the consumer's judgement
Evaluating planning / brainstorm / review roles — harness only exercises the implement-and-verify role; the other roles need a different instrument
Persisting the comparison — run-record persistence is Task 19; this task consumes those records
task.body:
harness's dogfood loop produces a binary pass/fail verdict per run — it verifies that a task was delivered, but never measures or compares how well different agents perform. Every dogfood task to date has gone green without the repair loop firing, and each was dispatched on a different task to a single agent, so the accumulated runs cannot rank the agents: the only signal captured is did-it-pass. The missing piece that turns harness from a verifier into an evaluation instrument is a same-task A/B mode.

Add a mode that dispatches one rmap task to several agents concurrently — each driven in its own isolated worktree, exactly as a normal batch run — and collects the results into a side-by-side comparison rather than an ordered per-task list. The comparison surfaces the per-agent quality metrics harness already captures or can cheaply derive: the verification verdict, repair attempts, wall-clock duration, how many checks were red on the first verification attempt, and the size of the agent's diff. This is a variant of the existing batch fan-out (Task 9) — same fan-out and crash-isolation, but one task across N adapters instead of N tasks each on one adapter, with a comparison aggregator in place of the ordered result list. Reuse the batch machinery; do not build a second orchestrator.

The load-bearing design constraint: the verification stack stays the binary pass/fail grader. Evaluator separation means the agent never grades itself — and harness must not start grading on a fuzzy composite score either. Evaluation metrics are a separate, additive layer read off the run records; they inform the human's judgement, they do not become the verdict. The run-record fields the comparison reads (first-attempt failed-check count, agent diff size) are captured by Task 19; this task consumes them.

task.title: Audit-surfaced: Batch.fill_slots crashes after AgentRegistry exhaustion
acceptance_criteria: A batch where all capable adapters are quota-exhausted mid-flight settles every queued item as a failed result and returns a Harness.Batch.Result
Regression test in test/harness/batch_test.exs covers the exhausted-mid-flight path
out_of_scope: Persistent registry availability across crashes (separate audit follow-up)
task.body:
`Harness.Batch.fill_slots/6` (after the Task 16 fail-over wiring) calls `AgentRegistry.select/2` and unconditionally pattern-matches `{:ok, adapter} = AgentRegistry.select(...)`. After every capable adapter has been marked unavailable by quota fail-over, `select/2` returns `{:error, {:no_available_agent, _}}` and the unmatched `:error` tuple crashes the batch process with a `MatchError`. Active runs become orphaned and the batch's caller never receives a `Harness.Batch.Result`.

Reproduction sketch: dispatch a 3-item batch with 1 capable adapter; have the first item exhaust quota so it fails-over but no adapter is available; the loop crashes when fill_slots tries to dispatch item 2.

Resolution candidates: (a) handle the `{:error, _}` from `select/2` by settling the queued items as failed `Run.Result`s with reason `{:no_available_agent, _}` and continuing the loop; (b) make selection + dispatch atomic via a registry-reservation API (also fixes the sibling race below). Add a regression test: 2+ items, 1 quota-exhausted adapter, no further capable adapters.

Filed by audit-review against commit 9b686a9b on 2026-05-23; see `.audit/9b686a9-agent-registry.md` (Claude+Codex agreed; bug exists in committed code). Companion to the next task ("Batch.fill_slots race on start_run").
task.implemented: Refactored Batch.fill_slots (/6 → /8) to thread results+events accumulators and case-match AgentRegistry.select/2. On {:error, reason}, calls settle_undispatchable to fold the remaining queue into failed Run.Results with reason: {:no_available_agent, reason} and emits per-item :no_available_agent events instead of crashing with MatchError. Added regression test 'settles queued items when every capable adapter is quota-exhausted mid-flight'. Verified by harness verification stack in worktree run-1779522372220-6be0341b: test/dialyzer/credo/doctor/sobelow all green; re-verified post-integration on development.

task.title: Audit-surfaced: Batch.fill_slots race — start_run errors crash the batch
acceptance_criteria: start_run/4 errors in Batch.fill_slots are handled without crashing the orchestrator
Concurrent-batch race regression test (or a test that simulates the start_run error path)
task.body:
`Harness.Batch.fill_slots/6` pattern-matches `{:ok, run_id, pid} = RunSupervisor.start_run(item, repo, adapter, run_opts)`. After Task 16, `Run.Supervisor.start_run/4` re-checks `AgentRegistry.select/2` and can return `{:error, {:no_available_agent, _}}` if another concurrent batch marked the adapter unavailable between `Batch`'s select and the supervisor's re-check. The unmatched `:error` tuple crashes the batch process.

Resolution candidates: (a) treat `start_run/4` errors as a dispatch failure and re-attempt selection within the same `fill_slots/6` recursion before failing the queued item; (b) make selection and dispatch atomic via a `reserve_then_start` registry API. Currently the race window is narrow (sub-millisecond) but real under concurrent batches sharing adapters.

Filed by audit-review against commit 9b686a9b on 2026-05-23; see `.audit/9b686a9-agent-registry.md`. Companion to the previous task ("Batch.fill_slots crashes after AgentRegistry exhaustion").
task.implemented: lib/harness/batch.ex fill_slots/6 wraps start_run/4 in a case with {:no_available_agent, _} (retry) and {:error, reason} (settle_start_run_failure) branches; regression test (run-1779588540022-c798e382)

task.title: Audit-surfaced: Harness-injected rule files get committed by Worktree.commit
acceptance_criteria: A no-op agent run for Claude/Codex/Cursor settles :no_changes (harness-injected rule files do not turn into a delivery commit)
Regression test per affected adapter covering the no-op path
Existing AGENTS.md in the target repo (if any) is not modified by the harness-injected block ending up in the run's delivery commit
task.body:
After Task 22, `Harness.AgentAdapter.RulesInjection` writes rule files into the run worktree at `build_command/1` time: `.harness/agent-rules.md` (Claude), `AGENTS.md` (Codex), `.cursor/rules/harness-operational.mdc` (Cursor). `Harness.Worktree.commit/2` stages every change with `git add -A` before committing, so these harness-owned files end up in the agent-delivery commit:

  - An agent that makes **zero** edits still has rules files in the worktree -> `git status --porcelain` is non-empty -> `commit/2` returns `{:ok, :committed}` instead of `{:ok, :no_changes}`, and the deliverable is the harness-injected rule files alone.
  - Target repos that had no `AGENTS.md` get a harness-prepended one in `harness/<id>`'s tree; target repos that had one get the harness block prepended (then committed).
  - Cursor's `.cursor/rules/` file lands in the deliverable similarly.

Resolution candidates: (a) write rules outside the worktree where the adapter allows (Claude's `--append-system-prompt-file` accepts an absolute path, so a `tmp_dir`-based file works); (b) add a pathspec exclusion to `Worktree.commit/2`'s `git add` (e.g. `git add -A -- ':!:.harness' ':!:.cursor/rules/harness-operational.mdc' ':!:AGENTS.md'`) — but `AGENTS.md` exclusion would also drop legitimate agent edits to that file; (c) clean up the harness-owned files between agent termination and commit; (d) write to a worktree-local untracked path and configure `.git/info/exclude` per run.

Regression test: an adapter `build_command/1` for each of Claude/Codex/Cursor + `Worktree.commit/2` over a no-op agent run settles `:no_changes` (not `:committed`).

Filed by audit-review against commit 826aaff3 on 2026-05-23; see `.audit/826aaff-harness-owned-rule-set.md` (Codex Pri 9, Claude verified Worktree.commit uses `git add -A`).
task.implemented: Added Harness.AgentRules.cleanup_injected_rules/1 (deletes Claude/Cursor rule files; strips harness block from AGENTS.md while preserving legitimate Codex content). Worktree.commit/2 and Worktree.diff_size/1 call it before staging so injected rules never reach the agent's branch. Closeout: also added sobelow_skip annotations on three new helpers (paths built via worktree_file!/2 — false-positive class).

task.title: Audit-surfaced: Repair loop ignores quota classification before resuming
acceptance_criteria: A repair-loop test where the resumed agent's output matches the quota patterns settles the run as failed without burning all configured attempts
Repair-loop quota detection uses the same RetryPolicy / FailureClass surface the batch fail-over relies on
task.body:
`Harness.Run.repairable?/1` checks only `data.repair_attempts < data.max_repair_attempts` and the adapter's `:session_resume` capability. It does not consult `Harness.Run.FailureClass`/`Harness.Run.RetryPolicy` quota patterns on the agent's outcome before deciding to resume. A quota-starved agent whose output triggers the quota patterns will still be resumed up to `max_repair_attempts` times — wasted attempts that may also bill against the same quota.

The `:no_changes` fast-path partially mitigates this (a quota-starved agent that produces no diff settles `:no_changes` at attempt 1, per the existing test `a non-repairable failure ends the loop without burning the attempt budget`). But an agent that produces some output before the quota cap is hit (e.g., a partial transcript with a quota error inline) still drives the repair loop pointlessly.

Resolution candidates: (a) classify the failed `verdict`+`agent_outcome` with `FailureClass.classify/2` inside `repairable?/1` and treat `:quota_exhausted` as non-repairable; (b) tighten the `:no_changes` short-circuit to also fire on output-but-no-diff quota errors.

Filed by audit-review against commit 348acb1b on 2026-05-23; see `.audit/348acb1-batch-orchestrator.md`.
task.implemented: lib/harness/run.ex repairable?/1 + lib/harness/run/supervisor.ex now classify FailureClass before resuming the repair loop so quota-exhaustion verdicts skip repair; regression test + fake_adapter support (run-1779588540033-8df8da06)

task.title: Audit-surfaced: Batch slot held until terminal_linger expires
acceptance_criteria: A two-item, max_concurrency=1 batch completes within materially less than 2 * terminal_linger of the runs' true settle time
Crash handling still produces a Run.Result with reason {:run_crashed, _}
task.body:
`Harness.Batch.loop/5` waits for the run's `:DOWN` message before freeing a slot — it stores the `Harness.Run.Result` on the active run (via `put_result/3`) when the `{:harness_run, run_id, result}` message arrives but only calls `settle_down/8` (which deletes the active entry and frees the slot) on `:DOWN`. Because `Harness.Run` lingers `:terminal_linger` ms (default 5_000) after settling before exiting, the slot stays occupied for that linger window even though the result is already known.

For a max-concurrency-of-1 batch this means up to 5s of idle wall-time between every two runs.

Resolution: treat `{:harness_run, run_id, result}` as the slot-settling event — demonitor and remove from active there — and reserve `:DOWN` handling for crashes without a result (the current `crashed_result/3` path).

Filed by audit-review against commit 348acb1b on 2026-05-23; see `.audit/348acb1-batch-orchestrator.md`.
task.implemented: lib/harness/batch.ex receive loop treats {:harness_run, run_id, result} as a settle event (settle_result/7 demonitors + Map.delete on the active slot), reverting the broken put_result that held the slot until terminal_linger; result field dropped from active_run typep; regression test (run-1779588540011-f4b6e4a3)

Either the behaviour callback set or ConformanceCase encodes the rule-injection contract
task.body:
After Task 22, every adapter's `build_command/1` calls into `Harness.AgentAdapter.RulesInjection` (one of `claude_flags/1`, `install_codex_rules/1`, `install_cursor_rules/1`, or `prepend_prompt/1`). The wiring is hand-replicated across all five adapters; nothing in the `Harness.AgentAdapter` behaviour callbacks or the `Harness.AgentAdapter.ConformanceCase` suite requires it. The next adapter implementor can omit the rules injection silently, and no test will catch it.

Resolution candidates: (a) add a behaviour-level optional callback for rule delivery (e.g. `c:rule_channel/0` returning `:system_prompt_file | :ephemeral_file | :prompt_preamble`) so `AgentAdapter.invoke/2` handles injection generically; (b) extend `ConformanceCase` with a test that gates `build_command/1` output for the presence of injected rules in the argv/env/cwd file system (a clone-backed `mix reach.check --smells` rule may also help). Companion to Task 27 (hoist universal adapter callbacks into the behaviour).

task.title: Audit-surfaced: AgentRegistry availability lost on GenServer restart
acceptance_criteria: A decision is recorded on which of (a)/(b)/(c) is the contract
If (a): persistent state survives a forced restart of AgentRegistry, validated by a regression test
If (b): @moduledoc and CLAUDE.md state explicitly that registry restarts clear quota state, and orchestrator-side retries cover misdirected dispatches
task.body:
`Harness.AgentRegistry` keeps unavailability (quota-exhausted, manually marked unavailable) in `GenServer` state only — `init/1` boots with `unavailable: %{}`. A supervised restart (the registry is started as a child of `Harness.Application` with default restart strategy) resets the table and a known-quota-exhausted adapter becomes available again on the next `select/2`. There is no persistence and no TTL on quota state.

Resolution requires a deliberate contract decision (this is `discuss-design`):

  - (a) Persist unavailability across restarts (e.g., DETS, persistent_term, or :ets owned by a different process). Survives crashes but complicates testing and adds startup ordering.
  - (b) Document the reset semantics explicitly and rely on the registry being treated as fail-stop infrastructure (an orchestrator-level retry catches misdirected dispatches).
  - (c) TTL-based "soft" unavailability (auto-reset after the typical quota-window).

Filed by audit-review against commit 9b686a9b on 2026-05-23; see `.audit/9b686a9-agent-registry.md`. Codex flagged this as `discuss-design`; Claude agrees the design decision belongs to the user.

task.title: Codex adapter — worktree isolation breaks intermittently (cwd ignored, agent edits main checkout)
acceptance_criteria: A Codex-driven harness run edits files only inside its run worktree across all run shapes (single, batched, parallel multi-driver)
The mechanism behind the empty-worktree-at-startup observation is identified and documented (race condition, fallback heuristic, or both)
The mechanism behind the disappearing-worktree-at-finalize observation is identified and fixed
A regression test exercises Codex in a parallel batch and asserts the main checkout is unchanged after settle
If Codex cannot be reliably constrained, dispatch fails fast with a clear error and the main-checkout-pollution failure mode is impossible
out_of_scope: Fixing the codex CLI upstream — harness works with the CLI as shipped
Antigravity adapter — already tracked under Task 32
Other adapters (Claude, Cursor, Grok) — they isolated correctly in Round-3a and prior batches
task.body:
During Round-3a (2026-05-23), Task 19 was driven by the Codex adapter. harness Port-spawned `codex exec --json --dangerously-bypass-approvals-and-sandbox` with the port `:cd` set to the run's isolated worktree, but Codex edited files in the *main checkout* (`~/_DATA/code/harness/`) instead — the run settled `{:commit_failed, {:git_failed, ["add", "-A"], 128, "fatal: cannot change to '...run-1779522372240-55f9e5f3': No such file or directory"}}` because by the time harness ran its commit step, the worktree directory was gone. Codex's transcript made the failure mode explicit: *"the assigned run worktree path was empty, so I used the actual harness checkout I found."*

Codex's Task 19 implementation was real and self-graded green — 280 tests, format / credo / doctor / sobelow / dialyzer all clean — but the diff (~701 lines across 11 files) landed in the canonical checkout, ungraded by the harness verification stack. It was hand-integrated onto `development` post-hoc, with conflicts in `batch.ex` and `batch_test.exs` against Task 34 resolved manually.

**Key signal: this is a regression, not a stable trait of the adapter.** Codex worked cleanly in Round-2 (Task 16, 2026-05-22) — same adapter, same worktree mechanism, no main-checkout leak. So either (a) something in the Round-3a run shape triggered a code path Round-2 missed, or (b) there's a race in worktree provisioning that fires only under certain conditions (parallel runs? specific dispatch ordering?).

Two intertwined questions to investigate:
1. **Why did Codex see an empty worktree at startup?** The Port's `:cd` was set; if the dir existed but was empty (no files yet), Codex's fallback heuristic kicked in. If the dir was missing, the Port spawn should have failed.
2. **Why was the worktree gone at finalize time?** harness emitted `worktree finish failed for ...run-1779522372240-55f9e5f3: {:marker_write_failed, "...": :enoent}` — confirming the dir was missing when the run tried to clean up. Did harness's own `Worktree.create` race against `Worktree.sweep` / boot-sweep? Did another sibling run's teardown stomp on it? Did `git worktree add` succeed but never actually persist files?

Per Task 32's precedent: if Codex cannot be headlessly constrained to a single directory under all conditions, gate Codex dispatch behind a startup check that detects the failure and fails fast with a clear error rather than silently polluting the main checkout. A regression guard (test or runtime check) catches future adapters that write outside their run worktree.

Mirrors Task 32 (Antigravity worktree-isolation bug) — same failure surface, different agent. Resolution shape should generalize.

task.title: Dogfood verification reds on pre-existing TODO comments in dispatch base
acceptance_criteria: Dispatched run does NOT red on TagTODO when the only TODO is in the dispatch base (not introduced by the agent)
Regression test: dispatch base contains a `# TODO(...):` comment, agent's diff adds no TODOs, verification passes
Dispatched run STILL reds on TagTODO when the agent ADDS a new TODO that was not in the dispatch base
out_of_scope: Changing audit-review's TODO format (this fix is harness-side, not staged-review-side)
Stripping TODOs from the dispatch base
task.body:
When `staged-review:audit-review` runs on the default branch, it sometimes records a follow-up by inserting a literal `# TODO(Task NN): ...` comment into the source (e.g. audit commit 6a01b58 added `TODO(Task 35)` to `lib/harness/batch.ex`). Dispatched dogfood worktrees fork off HEAD on `development`, so they inherit those TODOs. The verification stack runs `mix credo --strict`, which fails the run on TagTODO — penalizing the dispatched agent for pre-existing debt unrelated to their task.

Concrete impact, Round-3b: 4 of 5 dispatched tasks (29, 30, 37, 38) reded on their first verification pass solely because of the inherited `TODO(Task 35)` comment, then spent their repair cycle removing the comment instead of doing real task work. Task 35 (Cursor) absorbed it naturally because its implementation removed those exact lines.

Resolution candidates: (a) harness's verification stack tolerates TODOs that pre-exist in the dispatch base (diff-aware credo: only fail on TODOs introduced by the agent); (b) harness dispatches off a "clean" ref (last commit before any audit) rather than HEAD; (c) audit-review records follow-ups in a format that doesn't trip TagTODO strict (e.g. `# AUDIT-FOLLOWUP(Task NN):` instead of `# TODO:`).

(a) is the cleanest — preserves audit-review's existing UX and doesn't require dispatchers to maneuver around recent audits.
task.implemented: Worktree handle now captures :base_sha at carve-out (used as the diff baseline). Verification.Check gains an optional post_process hook; new Harness.Verification.BaselineFilter.Credo invokes 'git diff --name-only base..HEAD' to get changed files, parses credo's JSON, and drops TagTODO findings outside those files (i.e. inherited debt). Verification.run/2 threads :base_ref through post_process_opts. Closeout: added :jason to dialyzer plt_add_apps (new lib/ caller); fixed t:post_process/0 doc-ref shape.

task.title: Promote check stack to a first-class %Harness.CheckStack{} with a preset library
acceptance_criteria: %Harness.CheckStack{} struct defined with name, checks, optional parser, optional timeout_per_check
Harness.CheckStack.Preset.Elixir submodule exposes the current 5-check stack via preset/0 returning a %CheckStack{}
Harness.CheckStack.Preset registry module defines fetch/1 which dispatches to the per-language submodule (fetch(:elixir) → Preset.Elixir.preset/0); both must exist and be wired together
Harness.Verification.run/2 accepts a %CheckStack{} and produces the same %Verdict{} shape as today
Existing callers passing :checks opt continue to work (back-compat preserved during this task)
Dogfood-grade tests covering preset fetch, custom-stack run, and back-compat path
out_of_scope: Rust preset (Task 45)
Per-project check-stack storage (Task 46)
Dashboard rendering (Task 50)
task.body:
The verification stack today is `@elixir_preset` — five hard-coded `mix` commands inside `Harness.Verification`. Custom checks can be passed via the `:checks` opt, but there's no first-class "this is a Rust check stack" or "this is the Elixir preset" concept. That makes per-project verification configuration awkward and blocks the Rust preset (Task 45) and the project registry (Task 46) from carrying verification declaratively.

Introduce `%Harness.CheckStack{name, checks, parser, timeout_per_check}` as a first-class struct. Extract the current `@elixir_preset` into a `Harness.CheckStack.Preset.Elixir` module. Create a `Harness.CheckStack.Preset` registry so callers can fetch `CheckStack.Preset.fetch(:elixir)` and pass the resulting `%CheckStack{}` to `Verification.run/2`. Verification continues to accept either a `%CheckStack{}` or a raw `:checks` list (back-compat for existing callers in this task; eventually `%CheckStack{}` becomes the canonical input).

This is the foundation Tasks 45 (Rust preset), 46 (Project carries `:check_stack`), and 50 (dashboard renders per-project verdicts) all build on.

task.title: First non-Elixir preset: Rust check stack
acceptance_criteria: Harness.CheckStack.Preset.Rust.preset/0 returns a %CheckStack{} with at minimum: cargo fmt --check (role: format), cargo clippy -- -D warnings (role: lint), cargo test --message-format=json (role: test), cargo build --release (role: build)
Harness.CheckStack.Preset.fetch(:rust) returns it

Test covers both green (passing fixture) and red (intentionally-broken fixture) paths
No Elixir-specific assumptions remain in Harness.Verification after this task

Python, TypeScript, or other presets (file separately when demand exists)
Project struct (Task 46)
task.body:
Validate the `%Harness.CheckStack{}` abstraction by adding the Rust preset as the first non-Elixir verification target. The Rust preset should run the canonical Cargo check stack: format check, clippy with warnings-as-errors, tests with structured output, release build.

The point of this task is not "support Rust comprehensively" — it's to prove the check-stack abstraction holds up under a real second target. If anything in `Harness.Verification` or `%CheckStack{}` had a latent Elixir assumption, the Rust preset surfaces it.

Use `cargo test --message-format=json` so that future per-check parsers (e.g. extracting failed test names from cargo's JSON output) have something structured to work with. Don't write the parser in this task — just emit and capture the raw output, same as the Elixir preset does today.

task.title: %Harness.Project{} struct + in-memory ProjectRegistry; Run takes Project
acceptance_criteria: %Harness.Project{} struct with name, source, check_stack, roadmap_path, concurrency_cap fields
Harness.ProjectRegistry GenServer with register/1, lookup/1, list/0, unregister/1
Harness.Application starts ProjectRegistry as a supervised child
Harness.Run.start_link/1 accepts {%Item{}, %Project{}, adapter, opts} (old repo-string form no longer works)
Harness.Batch.run/4 accepts a %Project{} or a registered project name
Harness.Worktree.create/2 derives base path from project name
Harness.Roadmap.ingest/2 honors project.roadmap_path when given a project
All existing tests pass after migration
A test demonstrates two %Project{}s registered with different check_stacks running concurrently in the same node, each producing the verdict its own check_stack dictates
out_of_scope: GitHub-URL source (Task 47)
Two-tier concurrency enforcement (Task 48 builds on the per-project cap field added here)
Persistence of registered projects across node restarts (in-memory only; persistence can be filed as a follow-up if needed)
task.body:
Today every layer of harness implicitly assumes one project: `Harness.Run.start_link/1` takes `{%Item{}, repo, adapter, opts}` where `repo` is a bare path string, `Harness.Batch.run/4` takes one `repo` per batch, and the worktree base is rooted under `~/_DATA/worktrees/.harness/<repo-basename>/`. To orchestrate N projects concurrently, the project must be a first-class concept.

Introduce `%Harness.Project{}` with fields: `name` (unique slug), `source` (initially just `{:local, path}`; `{:github, url}` lands in Task 47), `check_stack` (`%Harness.CheckStack{}` from Task 44), `roadmap_path` (per-project rmap roadmap location), `concurrency_cap` (per-project cap; default nil = inherit global). Plus `Harness.ProjectRegistry` — a GenServer holding registered projects in-memory (registered at app start from config, or via `Harness.ProjectRegistry.register/1` for dynamic registration).

Migrate `Harness.Run.start_link/1` to take a `%Project{}` instead of a bare repo string. Update `Harness.Batch.run/4` to accept either a `%Project{}` or a project name resolved against the registry. Update `Harness.Worktree.create/2` callers to derive base from project name (`Path.basename(project.source.path)` continues to work for local sources). Update `Harness.Roadmap.ingest/2` to consume `project.roadmap_path` when called per-project.

Don't add a backwards-compat shim accepting both the old `repo` string and a `%Project{}` — do the migration cleanly. Update every callsite, every test. The Round-4 in-flight tasks (27, 28, 36, 43) are on existing surfaces and won't conflict with this migration since they predate it.

Concurrency note: at Task 46-time the per-project `concurrency_cap` field is wired into the existing `Harness.Batch.run/4` coordinator (in-memory, in-node). Task 48 replaces that coordinator with Oban queue-per-project, where the same `concurrency_cap` becomes the queue's concurrency setting. The field's shape doesn't change between 46 and 48; only the enforcement mechanism does.

task.title: Harness.Project.Source.Github: clone-and-cache + fetch-before-run
acceptance_criteria: Harness.Project.Source.Local and Harness.Project.Source.Github exist as variants of the source field
Harness.Project.Source.Github.url/1 and local_path/1 (or similar) resolve a GitHub source to its local cache path
First-run of a GitHub-source project clones to ~/_DATA/harness/projects/<name>/ (path configurable)
Subsequent runs git fetch before worktree creation
Recovery path: if the cache dir is missing, re-clone transparently rather than failing
Test using a real public GitHub URL (small fixture repo) covers clone, fetch, and recovery paths
Test verifies that worktree creation against a GitHub-source project succeeds end-to-end
out_of_scope: Credential management beyond what gh/SSH already provides
Non-default branches (main/master only)
Submodules, LFS, shallow clones
Cache eviction / cleanup policy (manual for now)
task.body:
Once `%Harness.Project{}` exists (Task 46), extend its `source` field to also accept `{:github, url}`. The first time a GitHub-source project is registered or run, harness clones it to a known cache path (e.g. `~/_DATA/harness/projects/<project_name>/`). Before every run, harness `git fetch`es to avoid running an agent against stale `main`.

Credentials piggyback on the host's existing `gh` CLI and SSH config — do not invent an auth layer inside harness. If `gh auth status` is green and the user can `git clone` the URL from a shell, harness can too via the same shell-out path it uses for everything else.

The clone-and-cache flow needs to handle: first-time clone (target dir doesn't exist), subsequent fetch (target dir exists, refresh `main`), and the "user nuked the cache" recovery (target dir missing on a project that was previously cloned — re-clone transparently). It does NOT need to handle: branch tracking other than `main`/default, submodules, LFS, or shallow clones (those can be follow-ups when a real need surfaces).

task.title: Oban-backed dispatch: queue-per-project + run-state persistence across restart
acceptance_criteria: Oban, Ecto, Postgrex added as runtime deps in mix.exs
Harness.Repo Ecto repo defined; Postgres config in config/runtime.exs
Oban migration generated, runnable via mix ecto.migrate
Harness.Oban supervised by Harness.Application; queues bootstrapped from ProjectRegistry.list/0 at boot, dynamically added when ProjectRegistry.register/1 is called
Harness.Run.Worker (Oban worker) spawns the existing Harness.Run gen_statem and threads its terminal state into Oban's return contract (:ok / {:snooze, _} / {:cancel, _})
Harness.Batch.dispatch/2 enqueues jobs into the project's queue and returns immediately (async)
Per-project concurrency enforced via Oban queue concurrency = project.concurrency_cap
Restart test: dispatch 5 jobs, hard-kill the BEAM node mid-run, restart, confirm pending/in-flight jobs resume without manual intervention
All existing Run / Batch tests pass after migration
Doc note in CLAUDE.md clarifying the dispatch-vs-in-run retry layering
out_of_scope: Oban Pro's Smart Engine (cross-queue global cap) — note as optional upgrade; current design accepts that global cap = sum of per-queue caps
Web-based job introspection — Oban Web embed is in Task 50
Cron-driven autonomous polling — Task 51
Replacing the custom Task-10 retry policy with Oban's retry (intentionally kept separate)
task.body:
Today `Harness.Batch.run/4` is a synchronous in-memory coordinator: spawn up to `:max_concurrency` Run GenServers, wait for results, exit. Two weaknesses surface as soon as harness orchestrates N projects: (1) fairness across projects requires a custom coordinator (originally drafted as a two-tier cap); (2) BEAM node death loses every in-flight run because state is purely in-memory. Both problems are exactly what Oban is built for, and Postgres is already running on the dev laptop.

Add Oban + Ecto + Postgrex as runtime deps. Create `Harness.Repo` (Postgres). Generate Oban's migrations and run them. Add `Harness.Oban` as a supervised child of `Harness.Application`. Define `Harness.Run.Worker` (an `Oban.Worker`) that takes a `{project_name, item_id, adapter_module}` payload and spawns the existing `Harness.Run` `gen_statem`, blocking until terminal state. On terminal `:passed` return `:ok`; on `:failed` with quota/transient classification return `{:snooze, seconds}` so Oban retries after delay; on `:failed` with permanent classification return `{:cancel, reason}`.

Replace `Harness.Batch.run/4` with `Harness.Batch.dispatch/2` which enqueues N Oban jobs (one per item) into the project's queue. Each registered project gets its own Oban queue: queue name = `"project_#{project.name}"`, queue concurrency = `project.concurrency_cap`. Global concurrency: with open-source Oban, the sum of per-queue caps is the effective ceiling — document this and let the user pick per-project caps that sum to laptop capacity. (Oban Pro's Smart Engine gives a true global cap across queues; flag as optional upgrade in the task body, do not require it.)

Persistence: because each run is now an Oban job, an in-flight run's job row survives BEAM restart. On restart, Oban automatically re-enqueues unfinished jobs and the worker re-spawns the Run gen_statem. The existing `Harness.ResultStore` (Task 19, done) writes final verdicts; this task adds a sidecar checkpoint table (or uses Oban's `meta` column) so a resumed worker knows what stage the previous attempt reached. Minimum acceptance: restarted runs do not silently lose progress — at worst they restart from the dispatch step, never silently disappear.

Custom retry policy (Task 10, done): keep it inside `Harness.Run` gen_statem. Oban's retry handles dispatch-level transient failures (quota); harness's retry handles in-run repair-loop attempts. Two layers, distinct concerns.

This is the *contributor convenience* recipe. The primary model is still the long-running app with registered projects (the user's solo workflow), but the in-repo subdir lets a project ship with harness self-contained.

Deliverable: `docs/in-repo-subdir-recipe.md` documenting the layout + `priv/templates/in_repo_harness/` containing the actual files a `mix harness.init --in-repo` task would copy in (the mix task itself can be a follow-up; for now just having the template scaffolded is enough).

task.body:
Harness's natural operational surface is a live dashboard, not a CLI snapshot. The state is already structured (`Harness.StatusView.snapshot/0` returns a structured payload; `classify/1` buckets runs into IN FLIGHT / REPAIRING / GREEN / RED). With Oban handling dispatch (Task 48), there's now also a rich job-queue view available via Oban Web. Best-of-both: custom LiveView for the harness-native concerns (project switcher, live transcript, multi-project view), embed Oban Web for raw job-queue introspection.

Add Phoenix + LiveView as runtime deps. Add `oban_web` as a runtime dep. Build a `Harness.Dashboard.Live` LiveView that lists all registered projects (project switcher), shows per-project pending/in-flight/done counts (from `Harness.StatusView` + Oban queue stats), shows a live "active runs across all projects" view, and supports per-run drill-down (current state, repair-loop iteration count, verification verdict, live stream-json transcript pane driven by PubSub from the run's port output).

Mount Oban Web at `/harness/oban` for queue-centric introspection (job rows, queue depth, scheduled/retrying/discarded states, retry-now controls). The custom LiveView owns the project-centric and live-transcript views; Oban Web owns the queue-centric view. Each does what it does best; the dashboard is the union.

Two consumption shapes: standalone (harness brings up its own minimal Bandit + Phoenix endpoint at localhost:4016/harness, config-gated, default-on in dev; reuses the tidewave port if it's already there); mountable (consumers with their own Phoenix endpoint add `live "/harness/*path", Harness.Dashboard.Live` and `oban_dashboard "/harness/oban"` to their router). Pattern reference: Oban Web, LiveDashboard, Tidewave itself — they all ship as mountable LiveViews with optional standalone runners.

Bandit dep shape: declare `{:bandit, "~> 1.x", optional: true}` so mountable consumers who already have their own Phoenix endpoint (typical Phoenix app) don't get a second HTTP server dragged in. The standalone Endpoint wraps its Bandit reference in `Code.ensure_loaded?(Bandit)`; if the consumer didn't add Bandit themselves, standalone mode logs a clear "add :bandit to your deps to use the standalone dashboard" message and the LiveView mountable path still works. Phoenix + LiveView + oban_web stay required runtime deps — the dashboard is a core deliverable of Phase 7, not an opt-in extra.

This task is intentionally one task even though it has multiple deliverables (custom views + Oban Web embed). The first slice that ships is a minimal dashboard (project list + run list + Oban Web at /oban); transcript pane and stream-json plumbing can be the second pass within the same task.

task.body:
Once Oban is in (Task 48), cron is essentially free — `Oban.Plugins.Cron` is open-source and ships with Oban core. This unlocks autonomous operation: "every N hours, poll each registered project's roadmap; if there's a pending task that fits the available adapters and the project's concurrency cap has headroom, dispatch it."

Define `Harness.Cron.RoadmapPoller` as an Oban worker scheduled via the cron plugin. On each tick: for each `%Project{}` in `ProjectRegistry.list/0`, call `Harness.Roadmap.ingest(:next, project_root: project.roadmap_path)`; if an item is returned AND the project's queue has headroom AND a capable adapter is available, enqueue a Run.Worker job. Tick frequency is configurable (default `0 */2 * * *` = every 2 hours; user can dial up/down per their preference for how autonomous they want this to be).

This task is intentionally low-stakes: the cron is opt-in via config (`config :harness, :cron_polling, enabled: false` by default). With it on, harness becomes a "while I sleep" worker — wakes up, picks the next task across all projects, dispatches it, the agent runs, the verification stack grades, the dashboard reflects it. Turn it off and harness reverts to manual-dispatch only.

parallel marker: this can be done independently of Tasks 49, 50 — they share no files.
